name: Chen Pengpeng Goose
summary: Chaoshan brine-poached goose (卤鹅) — the dish Shenzhen queues for.
note: Get the goose liver and a mixed platter. Lines start around 18:00; arrive 17:30 or take a number on Dianping and walk the mall.

name: Runyuan Siji Coconut Chicken
summary: Hainan coconut-water hotpot — clear, faintly sweet broth with free-range chicken.
note: The most Shenzhen thing you can eat. Drink the broth first, before anything else goes in. Dip sauce is 沙姜 + chilli + 小青桔.

name: Muwu BBQ
summary: Skewer chain that started in Shenzhen and now covers the country.
note: Lamb skewers, grilled chives, 烤茄子 with garlic. Cheap, loud, open late. The correct second stop after drinks.

name: Ba He Li Beef Hotpot
summary: Chaoshan beef hotpot — a dozen cuts, each blanched for a different number of seconds.
note: Ask for the cut-by-cut timing card or watch the table next to you. 匙柄 and 吊龙 are the ones worth the wait.

name: Tao Tao Ju
summary: Guangzhou teahouse brand, over a century old, doing all-day yum cha properly.
note: 虾饺, 流沙包, 凤爪, and the 马拉糕. Weekend brunch is a mob — go Tuesday morning instead.

name: Lei Garden
summary: The Michelin-standard Cantonese benchmark; roast meats and double-boiled soups.
note: Book ahead. The 老火汤 and the XO sauce fried rice are worth the price on their own.

name: Fei Da Chu
summary: Hunan's signature dish — pork fried with fresh green chilli — done as a single obsession.
note: Genuinely hot, not performative hot. Order rice; you will need it. Shenzhen has a huge Hunanese population and this is what they go to.

name: Nong Geng Ji
summary: Shenzhen-born Hunan country cooking; ingredients trucked in from Hunan farms.
note: Rustic farmhouse set-up, 土菜 done seriously. Good for a group, good for introducing someone to Hunan food.

name: Tai Er Pickled Fish
summary: One dish: fish in a sour-and-hot pickled-cabbage broth. No substitutions, no parties over four.
note: The no-groups-over-four rule is real and it keeps the queue moving. Chili oil goes in at the table.

name: Haidilao
summary: Sichuan hotpot plus relentless hospitality: free manicures, noodle dancing, birthday ambushes.
note: Open till dawn at most branches. The waiting area is a free snack bar — arrive early and eat there.

name: Banu Tripe Hotpot
summary: Hotpot that markets itself on broth and tripe rather than service — the anti-Haidilao.
note: 七上八下: seven dips up, eight down. Fifteen seconds, no more.

name: Dian Dou De
summary: All-day Cantonese tea service; trolleys, tiles, and a very traditional room.
note: Good solo at 10:00 with a newspaper. Ask for 普洱 or 铁观音 with the meal.

name: Jade Garden
summary: Maxim's Cantonese institution — seafood tanks, banquet rooms, flawless service.
note: Reliable for a family meal or hosting someone. The 蜜汁叉烧 is the safe showpiece.

name: Guangzhou Restaurant
summary: Another old Guangzhou name; dim sum plus roast meats at mid prices.
note: Their mooncakes are the ones locals actually gift at Mid-Autumn.

name: Tao Heung
summary: Hong Kong-style yum cha, large halls, fast turnover.
note: Best value dim sum on this list. Go with four people and order broadly.

name: Shundegong
summary: Shunde cooking — the district Cantonese chefs come from. River fish, silky steamed eggs, double-skin milk.
note: Order 双皮奶 for dessert. It is the reason Shunde is famous.

name: Ocean Court
summary: Palace-scale Cantonese seafood restaurant, built for banquets.
note: Live tanks; you pick the fish. Price is by weight, so ask before it's cooked.

name: Chao Shang Chao
summary: Chaoshan seafood and cold plates — marinated crab, raw shrimp, braised platters.
note: The 生腌 (raw-marinated) section is a rite of passage. Strong stomachs only.

name: Fu He Cheng Beef Balls
summary: Hand-pounded Chaoshan beef balls — the ones that actually bounce.
note: A bowl of beef-ball noodle soup is a 25-yuan lunch that beats almost anything else at that price.

name: Guantang Beef Hotpot
summary: Neighbourhood Chaoshan beef hotpot, no frills, meat cut in front of you.
note: This is what the local version looks like — plastic stools, better meat, half the price of the mall branches.

name: Hakka King
summary: Hakka staples: stuffed tofu, salt-baked chicken, braised pork with preserved vegetables.
note: 深圳's eastern districts are Hakka country. 盐焗鸡 arrives whole and is best eaten with your hands.

name: Hakka Language
summary: Modern, mall-based take on Hakka cooking — cleaner room, same dishes.
note: Easier entry point to Hakka food than the village restaurants, and consistent.

name: Guangming Squab
summary: Roast squab from Guangming's state dairy farm — Shenzhen's own famous local dish.
note: Worth the 40-minute trip north. Eat it at the source in 光明, with the farm's dairy desserts after. Crisp skin, eaten whole.

name: Shajing Oysters
summary: Oysters from Shenzhen's western coast — grilled, dried, or in congee. Season runs roughly Nov–Mar.
note: Dried Shajing oysters are the traditional gift. Go in winter; in summer skip it.

name: Chaoshan Seafood Congee
summary: Clay-pot congee cooked to order with live shrimp and crab. The standard Shenzhen 夜宵.
note: Order it at 23:00 after drinks. It takes 30 minutes — that's the point.

name: Peijie Old Hotpot
summary: Chongqing-style beef-tallow hotpot, numbing and deeply savoury.
note: The 九宫格 grid is functional, not decorative — different cells are different temperatures.

name: Chen Xianggui
summary: Lanzhou hand-pulled beef noodles, made in front of you.
note: Specify noodle width: 毛细 is hair-thin, 大宽 is belt-wide. Free soup refill.

name: Ma Jiyong
summary: The other Lanzhou noodle chain — cleaner rooms, slightly richer broth.
note: Solid 30-yuan lunch anywhere in the city. Add the 卤蛋 and the lamb skewers.

name: Yin Ji Rice Rolls
summary: Cantonese 肠粉 — steamed rice sheets with shrimp, beef, or egg.
note: Breakfast food. The sweet soy poured at the table is what makes it.

name: Yu Jian Xiao Mian
summary: Chongqing street noodles — chilli oil, preserved vegetables, minced pork.
note: Order 干溜 (dry, no soup) if you want the sauce to actually coat the noodle.

name: Xi Jia De
summary: Northern dumplings, whole shrimp in each one, boiled to order.
note: Eat them with black vinegar and raw garlic the way the shop intends.

name: Hefu Noodles
summary: Noodle chain styled like a scholar's study — quiet, air-conditioned, book-lined.
note: The room is the reason to go. Free noodle refill for lunch-sized appetites.

name: Xin Rong Ji
summary: Taizhou seafood cooking, the most decorated restaurant group in China.
note: The 家烧黄鱼 is the dish. Book a week out and let them build the menu.

name: Da Dong
summary: Beijing roast duck, carved tableside, with the full pancake-and-condiment ceremony.
note: Order the whole bird for two; the leftovers become a second course.

name: Yong Fu
summary: Ningbo cuisine — cured and fermented seafood, quietly intense.
note: The 醉蟹 (drunken crab) is the reason this kitchen exists.

name: Da Shu Wu Jie
summary: High-end vegetarian tasting menu built to look and taste like meat.
note: Genuinely interesting even if you eat meat. Book the full course, not à la carte.

name: The St. Regis Shenzhen
summary: Hotel dining on the upper floors of KK100 — the highest restaurant tables in the city.
note: Go for afternoon tea and the view over Luohu, not for the food alone.

name: Park Hyatt Shenzhen
summary: Post-hou Bay tower with several strong restaurants and the best bar view in Nanshan.
note: The lobby lounge at sunset, facing Shenzhen Bay, is free if you only buy a drink.

name: Pasta la Vista
summary: Long-running Shekou Italian, the anchor of the expat dinner scene.
note: One of the few places in Shenzhen that has been serving the same Western food well for years.

name: Grafton's Irish Pub
summary: Irish pub in Shekou — live sport, Guinness, and the city's oldest expat crowd.
note: Best place in Shenzhen to watch a 3am Premier League match with people who also care.

name: Blue Frog
summary: Western chain — burgers, all-day breakfast, reliable and air-conditioned.
note: Not interesting, but it is the known quantity when you want an English menu and a coffee that isn't a project.

name: Wagas
summary: Healthy-casual chain: grain bowls, wraps, decent coffee.
note: Fine for a laptop lunch. Every mall has one, which is the appeal.

name: gaga
summary: Shenzhen-born all-day brunch and tea chain — the city's own answer to a café-restaurant.
note: Local brand, so worth supporting. The fruit teas are the signature and they are enormous.

name: Ippudo
summary: Hakata tonkotsu ramen, the Fukuoka original.
note: Ask for 硬め (katame) for firmer noodles. Free 辛子高菜 on the counter.

name: Korean BBQ Street
summary: Concentration of Korean restaurants around Luohu, serving the large local Korean community.
note: Look for the places full of Korean speakers — that's the filter, ignore the signage.

name: % Arabica
summary: Kyoto's minimal white-box coffee, with a Shenzhen Bay branch facing the water.
note: Go for the terrace and the Spanish latte. Queue is worst on weekend afternoons.

name: Gee Coffee
summary: One of the earliest specialty roasters in Shenzhen, in the creative park.
note: Single-origin pour-over, and a room full of designers. Good place to sit for two hours.

name: Seesaw Coffee
summary: Shanghai-born specialty chain; clean rooms, strong espresso programme.
note: Reliable flat white anywhere in the city. Tech-crowd default in Keyuan.

name: Manner Coffee
summary: Tiny kiosk coffee at genuinely low prices — the daily-driver option.
note: Bring your own cup for a discount. 15 yuan for a proper flat white is the best value in the city.

name: M Stand
summary: Design-led coffee chain; industrial rooms, oat-milk-focused menu.
note: The 燕麦曲奇拿铁 is the drink people order. Rooms are good for meetings.

name: OCT-LOFT Cafe Row
summary: A whole block of independent cafes in the converted factory park.
note: Come on a weekday afternoon, wander between three or four, and look at the galleries in between. This is the best aimless day in Shenzhen.

name: Nantou Ancient City Cafes
summary: Independent cafes tucked into a restored 1,700-year-old walled town.
note: Old village fabric, young tenants. The lanes are worth more than the coffee.

name: HEYTEA Lab
summary: The flagship format of the cheese-foam tea brand that Shenzhen turned into a global chain.
note: Order via the mini-program, never in the queue. 多肉葡萄 in summer, 芝芝莓莓 year-round.

name: Nayuki
summary: Fruit tea and soft European bread — founded in Shenzhen, now listed on the HKEX.
note: The big flagship stores have seating and bread, which makes them an actual café rather than a kiosk. Born here, so it counts as local.

name: Chagee
summary: Milk tea built on a real brewed tea base rather than powder.
note: 伯牙绝弦 is the order. Lighter and less sweet than the fruit-tea places.

name: Mixue Bingcheng
summary: Four-yuan ice cream, six-yuan lemonade. The largest tea chain on earth.
note: It is not good. It is four yuan. Both facts matter.

name: Bao Shifu
summary: Meat-floss cream buns (肉松小贝) — the snack with a permanent queue.
note: Buy one box, eat them the same day. The queue moves faster than it looks.

name: Holiland
summary: National bakery chain with an unexpectedly strong collab programme.
note: Their seasonal and character collaborations sell out in hours. Check the mini-program.

name: Lu Xi He
summary: Traditional Chinese pastry shop — 桃酥, egg yolk pastries, sold by weight.
note: Buy a mixed half-kilo by weight. This is the correct gift to bring to someone's parents.

name: Paul
summary: French bakery chain; proper croissants and baguettes.
note: When you need real butter and real bread, this is the dependable option.

name: Coco Park Bar Street
summary: Futian's open-air nightlife strip — a dense row of bars around the sunken shopping park.
note: This is where Shenzhen goes out. Starts slow at 21:00, peaks past midnight, and it's outdoors so it works most of the year.

name: Sea World Bar Street
summary: Bars and restaurants wrapped around the grounded Minghua cruise ship in Shekou.
note: More expat, more relaxed, better for a first date than Coco Park. Musical fountain at 20:00 and 21:00.

name: OCT Harbour Waterfront
summary: Canal-side bars and restaurants with a nightly water show.
note: Touristy but the setting is genuinely nice. Walk the canal loop after dinner.

name: Craftissimo
summary: Craft beer taproom in Shekou.
note: Shenzhen has a real craft scene now; this is one of the established rooms.

name: Rooftop Bars, Futian
summary: High-floor cocktail bars across the Futian CBD towers.
note: Go at 18:30 to catch the skyline at both daylight and lit-up. Cover charges apply on weekends.

name: B10 Live
summary: Shenzhen's best-known livehouse, in the OCT-LOFT creative park.
note: Check the schedule — indie, rock, and jazz most nights. Standing room, cheap tickets, real sound.

name: Shuiwei Village
summary: Dense urban-village food grid in Futian — cheap, late, and local.
note: The best 50-yuan dinner in the city. Walk the lanes, pick whichever place is full of people in work clothes.

name: Chegongmiao Food Street
summary: After-work eating and drinking strip serving the Futian office towers.
note: Busy 18:00–21:00, quiet after. Good for a casual group dinner near the metro.

name: Futian Agricultural Wholesale Market
summary: Working wholesale market — fruit, seafood, dried goods, at trade prices.
note: Go early morning. This is where you buy lychee in June and dried scallops for the year.

name: Dongmen Old Street
summary: Chaotic pedestrian shopping and street-food district — Shenzhen's oldest commercial core.
note: Overwhelming and completely worth one visit. Watch your pockets; eat the grilled squid.

name: Huaqiangbei Electronics Market
summary: The world's largest electronics market — ten floors of components, phones, and drones.
note: Not a food destination, but it is the single most Shenzhen thing a visitor can do. Go in the afternoon, bring cash, expect to be talked at.

name: Shenzhen Bay Park
summary: Thirteen kilometres of waterfront path facing Hong Kong across the bay.
note: Rent a bike and ride south at 17:30 for the sunset. Migratory birds on the mudflats in winter — bring binoculars if you care.

name: Shenzhen Talent Park
summary: Small waterfront park in Houhai, framed by the tech-district towers.
note: Best night skyline in the city — the towers light up and reflect in the water. Free, open late, ten minutes from the metro.

name: Lianhuashan Park
summary: Central hill park with the Deng Xiaoping statue and a kite-flying lawn.
note: Twenty-minute climb to the viewing platform for the full Futian CBD axis. Go at dusk; the light show starts after dark.

name: Bijiashan Park
summary: Quieter hill park next to Lianhuashan, with a good elevated walkway.
note: Less crowded than Lianhuashan and the views are nearly as good. The skywalk connecting to the north is worth doing.

name: Shenzhen Central Park
summary: Long green corridor running north-south through the middle of Futian.
note: Useful as a walking route rather than a destination — you can cross the district without touching a road.

name: Dasha River Greenway
summary: Restored river corridor with a continuous running and cycling path.
note: The best run in Shenzhen — flat, shaded, and it goes from the university down to the bay.

name: Xiangmi Park
summary: Futian's rose garden and lake park, next to the marriage registry.
note: Roses peak in spring. There is a book bar by the lake that's a genuine find.

name: Qianhai Stone Park
summary: Waterfront park in the new Qianhai financial district, with a large stone monument.
note: New, uncrowded, and the skyline across the water is still filling in — worth seeing now before it's finished.

name: Fairy Lake Botanical Garden
summary: Large botanical garden in the eastern hills, with Hongfa Temple inside it.
note: A full day. The temple is active and busy on weekends; the desert-plant and fern houses are the highlights.

name: MOCAPE — Museum of Contemporary Art & Planning
nameZh: 深圳市当代艺术与城市规划馆
summary: Two museums in one sculpted silver building by Coop Himmelb(l)au.
note: The architecture is the exhibit. Free, but book entry on WeChat in advance — it caps daily visitors.

name: Sea World Culture & Arts Center
nameZh: 海上世界文化艺术中心
summary: Fumihiko Maki's waterfront museum, home to Design Society's V&A partnership.
note: Best building in Shenzhen. The design exhibitions are strong and the roof terrace faces the sea. Combine with the bar street next door.

name: Shenzhen Museum
summary: Free city museum — the modern-Shenzhen galleries tell the fishing-village-to-megacity story properly.
note: Do the contemporary history floor, not the antiquities. It's the one that explains the city you're standing in.

name: He Xiangning Art Museum
summary: China's first museum named for a female artist, in OCT.
note: Small, free, and usually quiet. Good contemporary shows.

name: OCAT Contemporary Art Terminal
summary: Design and contemporary art space inside the OCT cultural cluster.
note: Part of the OCT gallery circuit — He Xiangning, OCAT, and the park are all a short walk apart.

name: Pingshan Art Museum
summary: Serious contemporary art museum out in the far east, with ambitious curatorial programmes.
note: An hour from Futian, and worth it when the show is good. Check what's on before committing to the trip.

name: Guanlan Printmaking Village
summary: Hakka village converted into an international printmaking base, with resident artists.
note: Old village architecture, working studios, very quiet on weekdays. Bring water — there's little to buy.

name: FreeSky Observation Deck
nameZh: 平安金融中心云际观光
summary: Observation deck on the 115th floor of the Ping An Finance Centre — 541 m, the tallest in Shenzhen.
note: Book the late-afternoon slot so you get day, sunset, and the lights in one ticket.

name: KK100 Tower
summary: Luohu's 442 m landmark, with hotel dining and bar floors near the top.
note: Better than the observation deck if you want a drink with the view rather than a ticket queue.

name: Shun Hing Square
summary: The 1996 tower that was once Asia's tallest — still the symbol of old Shenzhen.
note: Worth looking at from the street even if you don't go up. It's the city's first skyscraper era in one object.

name: Shenzhen Concert Hall & Library
summary: Twin Arata Isozaki buildings flanking the civic centre plaza.
note: The library's south wall of glass facing Lianhuashan is the reading room view to beat. Free to walk in.

name: Shenzhen Civic Centre
summary: The winged civic roof and the huge plaza at the centre of Futian.
note: Come at night for the coordinated building light show across the CBD skyline.

name: Shenzhen Bay Sports Centre
summary: The 'Spring Cocoon' stadium, wrapped in a steel lattice shell.
note: Best seen from the Talent Park side at night, when the lattice is lit.

name: OCT-LOFT Creative Park
summary: Former electronics factories turned into galleries, studios, cafes, and B10 livehouse.
note: The best half-day in Shenzhen. Wander, drink coffee, see a show at night. Weekday mornings are the quiet version.

name: Nantou Ancient City
summary: A 1,700-year-old walled town, carefully regenerated into a design and retail district.
note: Proof that Shenzhen is older than its reputation. The city-gate wall, the lanes, and the small museums are all free.

name: Dafen Oil Painting Village
summary: The village that once painted most of the world's reproductions, now half atelier, half gallery.
note: Completely unlike anywhere else. Watch painters work, commission a copy of anything, walk out with it in a tube.

name: Gankeng Hakka Town
summary: Restored Hakka village with traditional architecture and a small-town street layout.
note: Prettier at night when it's lit. Touristy, but the Hakka architecture is genuine.

name: Zhongying Street
summary: The 250-metre street where one side is Shenzhen and the other is Hong Kong.
note: You need a permit and your passport to enter — arrange it in advance. The border stones are the point.

name: Jiaochangwei
summary: Beach village of guesthouses next to Dapeng Fortress — Shenzhen's weekend escape.
note: Stay overnight rather than day-tripping; the beach is average but the village at night is the draw. Book early for holidays.

name: Dapeng Fortress
summary: Ming-dynasty military garrison town, one of the best-preserved in Guangdong.
note: Combine with Jiaochangwei next door. Old stone lanes, city walls, and almost no traffic.

name: Value Factory
summary: A 1980s float-glass factory converted into an exhibition and event space.
note: Brutalist industrial shell, good for events and design shows. Check what's running before going.

name: Kingkey Beer Factory
summary: Old Shenzhen brewery redeveloped into a retail and cultural block, keeping the fermenting tanks.
note: The retained steel tanks are the photo. New enough that it's still filling out.

name: Shenzhen Book City
summary: One of the largest bookstores in China, spread over several floors.
note: Free to browse for hours. There's an English section, thinner every year but still there.

name: Zhongshuge Bookstore
summary: The mirrored-ceiling bookstore chain — architecture first, books second.
note: Go for the photograph, stay if you like bookshops. Crowded on weekends.

name: Mi Bookstore
summary: Shenzhen bookstore chain with a café, events, and long opening hours.
note: Good rainy-day option with actual seating — rarer than it should be.

name: Wutong Mountain
summary: Shenzhen's highest peak at 944 m, in the hills above the east.
note: Three to four hours up. Cloud cover swallows the summit view most days — check the forecast or don't bother.

name: Tanglang Mountain
summary: City-edge hike in Nanshan with the tech district below and the bay beyond.
note: The right hike for a weekday evening — an hour up, metro at the bottom.

name: Maluan Mountain
summary: Eastern hill country with waterfalls and old villages, well off the tourist path.
note: Best after rain, when the falls are running. Long day, bring food and water.

name: Dameisha Beach
summary: Shenzhen's main public beach — free, long, and extremely crowded on holidays.
note: Free entry requires a booking in peak season. Go on a weekday or don't go at all.

name: Xichong Beach
summary: The longest and best beach on the Dapeng peninsula, with surf and a coastal trail.
note: The 东西涌穿越 coastal hike between Xichong and Dongchong is the best walk in Shenzhen. Start early, it's exposed.

name: Xiaomeisha
summary: Smaller, ticketed bay next to Dameisha, redeveloped with a resort and aquarium.
note: Calmer water than Dameisha and fewer people, but you pay for it.

name: Nan'ao Seafood Street
summary: Fishing-village seafood strip on the Dapeng peninsula; sea urchin is the speciality.
note: Pick from the tanks, agree the price per jin before it's cooked. Go for lunch and make a day of the peninsula.

name: Shekou Fisherman's Wharf
summary: Working fishing harbour and seafood market at the tip of the Shekou peninsula.
note: Watch the boats come in early morning. The market will cook what you buy.

name: Happy Valley Shenzhen
summary: The city's main theme park, with serious rollercoasters and a summer water park.
note: Go on a weekday. Queue times on holidays make it not worth the ticket.

name: Uniwalk Coastal City
summary: Nanshan's main mall and the pedestrian plaza around it.
note: The outdoor plaza at night is where Nanshan actually socialises. Good density of restaurants.

name: MixC World
summary: Open-air mall in Keyuan, designed as a walkable street grid rather than a box.
note: The best-designed mall in Shenzhen — outdoor lanes, so it works as a place to walk, not just shop.

name: Shenzhen Bay MixC
summary: The luxury mall, with the highest concentration of fine dining in the city.
note: Come for the restaurants rather than the shops. Basement food hall is surprisingly good value.

name: One Avenue
summary: Bao'an's enormous mall — one of the largest in the country by floor area.
note: You will get lost. That's half the fun, and the restaurant floors go on forever.

name: KK ONE
summary: Futian mall directly connected to the metro, heavy on food and young brands.
note: Practical choice — you can eat without going outside, which matters June to September.

name: Shangxiasha Village
summary: Urban village near the Futian border — dense lanes of cheap eats.
note: Same play as Shuiwei: follow the crowd, eat what they're eating, spend under 50.

name: Yuanling
summary: 1980s residential grid that has quietly become a cafe and small-shop district.
note: The most lived-in neighbourhood walk in Futian. Old banyans, small independents, no tourists.

name: Shenzhen North Railway Station
summary: High-speed rail hub, and the practical gateway from Guangzhou and Hong Kong West Kowloon.
note: Guangzhou is 30 minutes away, which makes a Shenzhen base genuinely useful for the whole delta.
